nodes.name: Eastern North Carolina barbecue
nodes.blurb: The whole pig, split and cooked over coals or on a gas or electric cooker, then chopped — skin, ham, shoulder, loin and belly together, 'every part of the hog except the squeal' — and dressed after cooking with a thin…

nodes.name: Lexington-style barbecue
nodes.blurb: Pork shoulders cooked slowly over hardwood coals, usually hickory, then chopped, coarse-chopped or sliced and dressed with a thin red sauce the Piedmont calls dip: vinegar, ketchup or tomato, water, salt, pepper and red…

nodes.name: Heavy tomato barbecue
nodes.blurb: Pork shoulders and butts, ribs and chicken cooked over hickory or on cookers and served with a thick, sweet, red sauce of tomato, brown sugar or molasses, vinegar and spices — the sauce the state tourism office says you…

nodes.name: Light tomato barbecue
nodes.blurb: Pork — whole hog in the Pee Dee, shoulders and hams in the upper Midlands — cooked over coals or on cookers and served with a thin sauce that is the Carolinas' vinegar-and-pepper with ketchup stirred in.

nodes.name: South Carolina mustard barbecue
nodes.blurb: Pork — whole hogs at some pits, hams or shoulders at others — cooked over hardwood coals or on cookers, chopped or pulled, and dressed with a yellow sauce of prepared mustard, vinegar, sugar and spices.

nodes.name: Pee Dee whole-hog barbecue
nodes.blurb: Whole hogs cooked overnight over hardwood coals, pulled or chopped, and dressed with a thin sauce of vinegar, salt, black pepper and red pepper — the same sauce as eastern North Carolina's across the state line.

nodes.name: Bone Suckin' Sauce
nodes.blurb: A Raleigh line of bottled sauces, of which the one that built the brand is Sweet Southern: cane sugar first, tomato puree second, water third, apple cider vinegar fourth, at six grams of sugar to the tablespoon.

nodes.name: Carolina Treet
nodes.blurb: A Wilmington sauce that fits none of the four Carolina bases. Its label reads water, vinegar, wheat flour, salt, soybean oil, paprika, garlic, onion, xanthan gum, spices — no tomato, no mustard, no sugar.

nodes.name: George's Barbecue Sauce
nodes.blurb: A bottled sauce from Nashville, North Carolina, a Nash County town on the edge of the Coastal Plain, sold in three strengths: Original, Hot and Special.

nodes.name: Golding Farms Foods
nodes.blurb: A Winston-Salem sauce manufacturer, the second of that city's two, and one whose output mostly reaches a table under someone else's name.

nodes.name: heavy tomato sauce
nodes.blurb: A thick red sauce built on tomato — ketchup, paste or sauce — sweetened with brown sugar or molasses, soured with vinegar and seasoned with spices, cooked down until it clings.

nodes.name: Lexington dip
nodes.blurb: The Piedmont's sauce: the east's vinegar, salt, pepper and red pepper with ketchup or tomato and water added, sometimes sugar, so that it comes out thin and reddish — tangy, a little sweet or hot by the house, and every…

nodes.name: light tomato sauce
nodes.blurb: Vinegar-and-pepper sauce with ketchup added — enough to redden and sweeten it a little, not enough to thicken it — and often cayenne or a bottled hot sauce.

nodes.name: Maurice's Southern Gold
nodes.blurb: The mustard sauce of Maurice's Piggie Park at West Columbia, sold in bottles, half gallons and gallons alongside the family's Hickory Red, Vinegar and Hot Pepper sauces.

nodes.name: Melvin's Golden Sauce
nodes.blurb: The mustard sauce of Melvin's Bar-B-Que in Charleston, sold in 16-ounce glass bottles, half gallons and gallons, beside the house's Southern Red, Sweet Red and Vinegar sauces.

nodes.name: mustard-based barbecue sauce
nodes.blurb: Prepared yellow mustard thinned with vinegar and sweetened with sugar or brown sugar, with black and red pepper and whatever else the house keeps to itself — Bessinger's bottled version listed mustard, brown sugar, soy…

nodes.name: Sam Jones BBQ sauce
nodes.blurb: A bottled line from the whole-hog house Sam Jones opened at Winterville in 2015, third generation of the Skylight Inn family at Ayden.

nodes.name: Scott's Barbecue Sauce
nodes.blurb: A bottled eastern North Carolina sauce — vinegar-based, the recipe kept secret, sold as sugar-free and fat-free — made by the Scott family of Goldsboro since the mid-1940s from a recipe the Rev.

nodes.name: Texas Pete
nodes.blurb: A cayenne-pepper hot sauce made by the T.W. Garner Food Company of Winston-Salem, North Carolina, since 1929 — mild as hot sauces go, 747 on the Scoville scale — in a flip-top bottle with a red cowboy on a…

nodes.name: vinegar-and-pepper sauce
nodes.blurb: Vinegar — cider or white — with salt, black pepper and crushed red pepper, and nothing else in its plainest form; some houses add sugar, a bottled hot sauce or lemon.

nodes.name: Wells Hog Heaven Barbecue Sauce
nodes.blurb: A vinegar-based sauce made at Burgaw, the seat of Pender County in southeastern North Carolina, and sold in that corner of the state.

nodes.name: baked beans
nodes.blurb: White beans — navy or pea beans — cooked slow in a sweet brown sauce of molasses or brown sugar with pork in it, and served hot in a cup or a compartment of the tray.

nodes.name: banana pudding
nodes.blurb: Layers of sweet vanilla custard, vanilla wafers and sliced bananas built up in a dish and topped with meringue or whipped cream, then chilled until the wafers soften and the layers run together.

nodes.name: barbecue chicken
nodes.blurb: Half a chicken, cooked on the pit beside the pig or on its own cooker until the skin chars, brushed with the house sauce — vinegar and pepper in the east, a thin tomato-and-vinegar dip in the Piedmont — and sold by the…

nodes.name: barbecue sandwich
nodes.blurb: Chopped pork on a soft white bun with slaw laid on the meat. In North Carolina it is the commonest form of the sandwich: whole-hog barbecue dressed with vinegar and pepper in the east, chopped or sliced shoulder with…

nodes.name: barbecue tray
nodes.blurb: The unit of ordering at a Carolina barbecue counter: a paper boat or a plate with the chopped pork on one side and slaw on the other, and no bun.

nodes.name: Blenheim Ginger Ale
nodes.blurb: A ginger ale bottled at Hamer, in Dillon County, South Carolina, made with Jamaica ginger and sugar in mineral water from a spring in Marlboro County, and hot enough that the heat is the point of it.

nodes.name: boiled potatoes
nodes.blurb: Potatoes boiled whole or in halves until they are soft and served beside chopped whole hog on the eastern North Carolina plate — the side the Piedmont does not have.

nodes.name: Brunswick stew
nodes.blurb: A thick tomato stew of chicken or pork with corn, butter beans (lima beans), onion and, in the east, potatoes, cooked in big pots and served in a cup beside the barbecue.

nodes.name: Cheerwine
nodes.blurb: A cherry-flavoured soft drink — burgundy-red, sweet, with a strong black-cherry note and more carbonation than most sodas — made in Salisbury, Rowan County, North Carolina by the Carolina Beverage Corporation since…

nodes.name: chicken bog
nodes.blurb: Chicken, rice and smoked sausage cooked together in the chicken's own broth until the rice has taken up the liquid and sits wet and plump — a pilau (rice cooked in stock) that is deliberately wetter than a pilau.

nodes.name: collards
nodes.blurb: Broad flat leaves of a loose-headed cabbage, stripped from the stem, cut in ribbons and stewed a long time with a piece of smoked pork until they are dark and soft, in a salty broth the South calls pot liquor.

nodes.name: cornbread
nodes.blurb: A quick bread of cornmeal — meal, water or buttermilk, salt, fat, often egg and soda — baked in a pan, a skillet or a stick mould. It comes with eastern North Carolina barbecue in two forms.

nodes.name: Duke's mayonnaise
nodes.blurb: A bottled mayonnaise made in Mauldin, South Carolina, outside Greenville: egg yolks, oil and cider vinegar, with more yolk than most brands and no added sugar, which is where the tang comes from that the company sells…

nodes.name: fried okra
nodes.blurb: Okra pods sliced into rounds, rolled in cornmeal and fried until the outside is crisp.

nodes.name: green beans
nodes.blurb: Whole or broken pods of the common bean, stewed slow with a piece of pork until they give up their squeak and take on the meat's salt, and served in a cup or a compartment beside the barbecue.

nodes.name: hash and rice
nodes.blurb: A thick stew, or gravy, of pork cooked down with onions until it can be eaten with a spoon, ladled over white rice beside the barbecue.

nodes.name: hushpuppies
nodes.blurb: Balls or fingers of cornmeal batter — meal, a little flour, egg, buttermilk or water, salt, soda, often onion — dropped by the spoonful into hot oil and fried until the outside is crisp and dark gold and the inside soft…

nodes.name: mac and cheese
nodes.blurb: Macaroni in a cheese sauce, most often cheddar, baked in a dish until the top browns.

nodes.name: outside brown
nodes.blurb: The dark crust from the outside of a pork shoulder — the bark, where ten hours of smoke and dip have cooked into the surface — ordered by name at Lexington pits.

nodes.name: peach cobbler
nodes.blurb: Sliced peaches sweetened and thickened in a deep dish and covered with a crust — pastry, biscuit dough or a batter — then baked until the top browns and the fruit bubbles at the edge.

nodes.name: pickles
nodes.blurb: Cucumbers held in brine or vinegar until they sour, sliced into rounds or spears and put on the plate beside the meat, with the sandwich, or loose in a dish on the table.

nodes.name: pig pickin' cake
nodes.blurb: A layer cake of convenience-food parts: yellow or butter-golden cake mix beaten with eggs, oil and a can of mandarin oranges, juice and all, baked in three eight-inch pans and frosted with a can of crushed pineapple…

nodes.name: pork skins
nodes.blurb: The pig's hide, cooked until it blisters and cracks. On an eastern whole hog the skin faces up through the night and is turned to the coals at the end to crisp; at Skylight Inn it is chopped into the meat, where the…

nodes.name: potato salad
nodes.blurb: Boiled potatoes cut up cold and dressed with mayonnaise, with hard-boiled egg, onion, celery, sweet pickle or relish and often a spoon of yellow mustard that colours the whole bowl.

nodes.name: red slaw
nodes.blurb: Finely chopped green cabbage dressed with vinegar, ketchup, sugar, salt and black pepper — or with the pit's own dip — and no mayonnaise.

nodes.name: sweet tea
nodes.blurb: Black tea brewed strong, sweetened with sugar while hot — so it dissolves, rather than being stirred into a cold glass — and poured over ice.

nodes.name: white slaw
nodes.blurb: Finely chopped cabbage in a dressing of mayonnaise or whipped salad dressing, sweet and pale: the slaw of eastern North Carolina and of most of South Carolina.

nodes.name: block pit
nodes.blurb: An open pit built above ground of cinder blocks — concrete blocks — wide and shallow, a little longer than a split hog, with a rack across the top on which the pig lies and a bed of charcoal below; brick or steel are…

nodes.name: brick pit
nodes.blurb: The masonry pit of the Piedmont: a closed brick chamber with a rack for the shoulders and a chimney through the roof to carry off the smoke.

nodes.name: burn barrel
nodes.blurb: A repurposed steel drum — or, at Scott's in Hemingway, two 55-gallon drums welded together — in which logs are burned down to coals: the wood goes in at the top, the coals are pulled out from below and carried by shovel…

nodes.name: chopping block
nodes.blurb: A thick wooden block and a pair of cleavers, on which cooked pork is turned into barbecue.

nodes.name: direct heat
nodes.blurb: The Carolina way of putting fire to meat: a bed of hardwood coals directly beneath the hog or the shoulders, with no flame and no separate firebox.

nodes.name: gas and electric cookers
nodes.blurb: The cookers most Carolina barbecue is cooked in: steel ovens fired by propane, natural gas or an electric element, with a thermostat and racks, and often a box for wood chips or a log to put smoke on the meat.

nodes.name: hickory and oak
nodes.blurb: The hardwoods of the Carolina pit. Hickory and oak are the woods a Carolina cook burns, usually together and usually burned down to coals before they go under the meat: Lexington pits cook over oak and hickory coals…

nodes.name: hog killing
nodes.blurb: The winter slaughter of the farm's hogs, done on the first cold day of autumn or winter, when the meat would keep.

nodes.name: pig cooker

nodes.name: whole hog

nodes.name: pig pickin'

facets.when: any month; homecomings, tailgates, weddings, rallies

nodes.blurb: A party at which a whole hog is cooked for the crowd and the crowd eats it off the pig — picked by hand from the split carcass, or chopped on a block beside it.

nodes.name: political barbecue

facets.when: election years; the weeks before a vote

nodes.blurb: The free feed a candidate or a party puts on to draw a crowd: a whole hog, or these days a pile of pork butts, cooked for whoever comes, with speeches or a rope line attached.

nodes.name: barbecue
nodes.blurb: The cooked meat itself — in the Carolinas, pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker and then chopped, pulled or sliced — and, by extension, the place that sells it and the gathering that eats it.

nodes.name: Carolina Gold

nodes.name: chopped
nodes.blurb: The way most Carolina barbecue reaches the tray: cooked meat cut across on a block with cleavers — in the east fine enough to hold the thin vinegar sauce, in the Piedmont in larger pieces.

nodes.name: dip
nodes.blurb: The Lexington word for its sauce: vinegar, water, ketchup or tomato, salt, black and red pepper, sugar to taste — thin enough to pour, reddish rather than red.

nodes.name: Down East
nodes.blurb: In North Carolina, the coastal plain east of Raleigh — the barbecue east, where the hog is cooked whole and the sauce has no tomato; eastern North Carolina barbecue is also called Down East barbecue.

nodes.name: Dutch Fork

nodes.name: fixins
nodes.blurb: The sides and trimmings that come with the meat: slaw, hushpuppies or cornbread, boiled potatoes in the east, hash and rice in South Carolina, pickles, sweet tea.

nodes.name: hog
nodes.blurb: In Carolina barbecue speech the animal is a hog. Whole hog is the eastern North Carolina and Pee Dee style; a hog killing is the winter work of the farm; a hog's size is its dressed weight.

nodes.name: light bread
nodes.blurb: The Southern name for white yeast bread — a store loaf or a soft bun — as against cornbread, biscuits and pone, a dense cornmeal cake.

nodes.name: Pee Dee
nodes.blurb: The river and the region. The Pee Dee rises in the North Carolina mountains as the Yadkin, takes the name Pee Dee below the mouth of the Uwharrie, crosses into South Carolina and reaches the sea at Winyah Bay.

nodes.name: Piedmont

nodes.name: pit
nodes.blurb: The place the cooking happens. First a trench in the ground filled with hardwood coals, the split hog on a rack above; then a wide, shallow container of cinder block, brick or steel above ground, still a pit; then, at…

nodes.name: pitmaster
nodes.blurb: The person who runs the pit — the fire, the coals, the turning of the hog, the call that it is done. A recent word for an old job.

nodes.name: pulled pork
nodes.blurb: Pork cooked slowly over coals or in a cooker until it comes off the bone in strands, then taken apart by hand or with forks rather than cut.

nodes.name: slaw
nodes.blurb: Shredded raw cabbage, dressed and served cold, on every Carolina barbecue tray and most sandwiches.

nodes.name: barbecue postcards
nodes.blurb: Between about 1930 and 1945 an American restaurant could order its own postcards by the thousand.

nodes.blurb: The Farm Security Administration — a New Deal agency for rural poverty — kept photographers on the road from 1935, and their negatives went to the Library of Congress as federal work, free of copyright.

nodes.name: the pig mascot
nodes.blurb: One pig, drawn once, used everywhere a barbecue business puts its name: the sign, the menu, the sauce label, the takeout box, the trailer door, the roofline, the weather vane.

nodes.name: Pigs in the City

nodes.name: Going the whole hog — the 1830s barbecue lithographs
nodes.blurb: A small group of American political prints from the 1830s in which the barbecue is the joke and the pig is the politician.

nodes.name: roadside barbecue signs
nodes.blurb: The sign a barbecue place puts at the road: a steel pylon with a lit box on top, neon or bulbs picking out a name, a bottler's disc above it, and a changeable letterboard underneath for the day's news.

nodes.name: How to order
aliases: what to say at the counter
nodes.blurb: At a Carolina barbecue counter the words are short and they mean particular things. Barbecue is the meat, not the event. A tray has no bread; a plate does.

nodes.name: The Great Divide
nodes.blurb: North Carolina cooks barbecue two ways and has never agreed to disagree about it. East of Raleigh the whole hog goes on the pit and the sauce is vinegar, salt and pepper with no tomato in it.
